items.text: Misti Y- points out you can love Cirque in general but not Le Reve, which is a separate discussion. For me Le Reve has been a letdown. It is an amazing theater. The visual design is the best part, the set design is beautiful from start to finish. The concept is appealing but it doesn't transfer to the live show very well. I went to a show and the stage kept malfunctioning the whole time. Hard to be engaged even during the more impressive parts. Le Reve is reaching for that showmanship and spectacle but never quite there. I'd go just to see the theater but otherwise I'd spend your money on another show.

The comfort is why I'm keeping it. Each key has a small bump partway down, so my fingers know a press registered without slamming to the bottom. I can get through a long email and my wrists feel fine after, which the flat laptop keys never managed. I paid $38 for this used mechanical keyboard and I think I got about $38 worth of keyboard, maybe a little more. The space bar rattles. Every thumb press gets a hollow clatter, like a tray of cutlery being nudged. I tune it out during the day but after midnight I find myself typing around it. The E key repeats now and then. "meeting" turns into "meeeting". It happens maybe once every few paragraphs. Rare enough to forget, frequent enough that I reread everything before hitting send. I messaged the seller to ask what switches it used, got tired of waiting, and bought it anyway. The answer came a week later, after the keyboard was already on my desk. Brown switches, for the record. I thought about sending it back. Return shipping would have eaten a real chunk of what I paid, and I'd be back on the laptop. So it stays, rattle and all.

Saw this circus-style theatrical show in Vegas and recommend it but taking one star off. The story's kinda hard to follow and a few songs are just wrong for the action, sleepy, not suitable. But the performers are just amazing. Very fit, athletic, good aerobic ability. The women are incredible - they stay under the water for minutes at a time. The stage is circular, the theater is circular, so all seats have a good view. There's three main entrances to the stage, they use them through the show and they're very important during the big transitions in the story. The stage and overall setting and lighting are beautiful, really memorable atmosphere. Tickets were reasonable in price, compared to major Vegas shows like O or Love. I wish there were more spectacular effects, especially fire, but that's not a big deal. But the story and music issues don't stop me from recommending. It's entertaining, very visually striking.

I spent two years mentoring five junior engineers and I think the idea that remote work is this universal cure all is overblown. Jrs don't really need tickets or docs or meetings. They need to sit in on design conversations, see others debug issues, ask questions in the moment. If the office is where it happens for me, for remote the jrs need to learn how to interrupt people, schedule calls, explain problems they don't even know how to describe. Its a skill to have when you havent had a chance to learn it. I have seen the feedback issues. Comments on code reviews are short and it feels like its the final word rather than a learning opportunity. Takes longer too, less momentum. The jrs I mentored were able to improve much faster if they had pairing, whiteboard sessions, and easy access to seniors. And I'm not pushing for offices or anti flexibility. For self driven devs it works. But for jrs the proximity is a booster. It gives you confidence, context, instinct. If you just send jrs off with a laptop and a calendar, its a drag on their development and less good technical leadership in the future.

Elias is working his kneading wrong. The note says he's left hand dominant, and that he should stop favoring the right. It's ruining the tension. He's been favoring right hand. He looks at his hands, red knuckled and dusted white. The mixer is on its next cycle. He closes the book and puts it back on the glass, spine aligned perfectly with the edge. Then he turns off the overhead light above the display, leaving the book in shadow. The book, The History of Salt, hardback, blue spine cracked near the hinge. It appeared every Thursday for six weeks, always on the glass display case next to the unsold cinnamon rolls. No library stamp. The bakery isn't a branch of the municipal system. Elias picked it up, the cover felt cold. He opened it and a folded square of lined notebook paper slipped out, landing on the counter with a soft tap. He unfolded it. The handwriting was jagged, pressed hard into the fiber. It was 3:17 AM. Flour dust hung in the air, catching the harsh fluorescent light like suspended snow. The sourdough loaves rested on wooden boards, pale and soft before the final bake. He wiped his hands on his apron, fabric stiff with dried dough and sweat. He moved to the front counter to check the lock, a ritual born of paranoia rather than necessity.

From my experience, Apple deserves a mention. School only let students use Apple laptops, even though they cost about twice as much as PC options. These things broke constantly. In my 4 years of use, I never dropped my laptop, but I had to replace the hard drive 5 times and repeatedly reinstall the operating system. A friend's MacBook Pro actually caught fire once while he was watching a movie, tripped the smoke alarm. Apple support couldn't diagnose any of the problems, just backed up the machine, wiped it and restored it. Criticism extends to iPhones. I had the first one and it malfunctioned all the time. Apple puts out a new iPhone every two months or so, and it's only slightly better on camera. Concession to one small positive: iPad is the best tablet for now, but Android tablets might catch up.

I grew up around Las Vegas, was dragged out there constantly before 21, saw tons of shows, so I know what these big theatre productions can be. The Wynn and Encore guest deal is nice, $99 instead of $125. If you’re staying at the Wynn or Encore, that’s a good deal.

It’s fine. Not a must-see I’d build a trip around. I’d say it’s just average. A few cool stunts, but nothing blew me away. My friends who saw it said they did enjoy it, so if you haven’t seen it, maybe check it out. But I wouldn’t see it again.

The story is unclear or nonexistent. I left with no idea what it was trying to say. But the story is a big issue, it’s not clear. The individual acts are impressive, the performers are strong as hell. Aerialists, acrobats, whatever. But I’ve seen them just as well in Cirque du Soleil shows.

It’s all very flashy. Stereotypical Vegas spectacle, more equals better. And that’s the problem. Too much going on, too many visuals, too many pieces, too many wow attempts. It’s messy. A more restrained production would hit harder. The circular stage is genuinely smart, you get a decent view from basically any seat, which is rare.

I wouldn’t pay full price again. And the thing is, more just meant messier. Not blown away.

Bought a skateboard at Zumiez, came back for rest of the gear. First bit seemed fine. Me, my friend, his little brother sat with a woman who called herself manager. She said she assembles boards every day. Said on bad days she was a shit to people. She took 90 min to put the thing together. I was thinking 15 min tops. She messed up 2 bolts, put them back in a way that made it look like she'd sell the stripped ones to another person. She finally got her brother, and another manager to help finish it. No apology. We are not coming back. My heart is broken.

Bought a mechanical keyboard second hand for $38. Seller communication was terrible, I asked about switch type before purchase, got a one word reply a week later after I already gambled on buying it. The board is well-loved, space bar rattles like a loose Lego brick, E key occasionally repeats. Typing 'the' becomes 'theee', kind of hilarious. But it's great for long emails. The tactile feedback is fantastic, very comfortable. Thought about returning it, but it's a heavy slab of plastic, more hassle than it's worth for $38. So I kept it. Grown fond of its flaws, so if you don't mind some DIY tuning and the double typing issue, it's a budget win.

Turkish Airlines is a nightmare. Booked Harbin Beijing domestic, then Turkish Beijing to Istanbul. Harbin got delayed, I missed connection, nobody at the desk took responsibility or helped rebook. Slept the night at airport. Next morning asked for a ticket, flights overbooked, takes days to get to Istanbul unless you pay for business. I needed Istanbul, so I paid. I'm furious, in complete disbelief.

So bring just one broken household item. Go to the desk on arrival, get the number that queues you.
It decides your turn so keep that number safe. Repairs are done by volunteer experts first come first served. You have to pick your item up before they leave at 4 PM. They won't store anything overnight. So make sure you have time to wait for your turn. No guarantee we can fix every device. But we can fix most. Thanks for following these simple rules so today's session runs smooth.

Float valves regulate troughs via a float on an arm, connected to a shutoff valve. When water level drops the float goes down, opens the valve and water starts to fill. As it fills, the float rises and closes the valve. At the set level it cuts off. So the water stops. Overflow can happen for 2 normal reasons. Debris or mineral buildup stops it from closing all the way. Or the float is set too high and it only closes after the trough is already overflowing.

Worst. It was Sunday, we got there at 7:20 p.m. We picked this place because we had a 10:00 p.m. show in the same hotel so it was just more convenient. We put our names in their useless digital waitlist and they told us to come back to pay at 8:23. So we went, stood around till 8:40 before someone casually said we'd probably not be seated until 9:15. It was just us, a party of two. No solutions at all. I can't even tell you if the food is good because we never got to eat. The night was completely wasted. If the wait is that far past payment you should just tell people upfront. Disaster. Zero stars if it were an option.

To all Enron employees.

The holidays are difficult this year. We have issues inside Enron and the world is scary. I know. We talked a lot about the holiday party on December 8. People were mixed. Some said it was a good idea, others said it was not appropriate. I understand both views. After what happened in the past month, we are canceling the party. Spending company money on a party now is imprudent. We should not take that risk. I'm sorry. You have worked hard. You deserve recognition and a reason to celebrate. We are looking for other ways to recognize your outstanding contributions during this holiday season. Ken Lay

A siphon moves water between containers by gravity and air pressure getting it over a peak. First you have to fill the tube so it holds one solid column of water. Then gravity pulls down the longer side. That low spot on top becomes a low pressure zone. Air pushing on the water where it starts gets more water up the short side.

The exit has to be below the starting water level. The source of force is that one column is heavier. If exit is high or same level there is no net pull, weight of the higher side doesn't beat the lower side.

When air bubbles come in it breaks the chain. The water molecules hold each other, that's how the pull works. Air breaks that chain. It equalizes the pressure inside with the outside air. The driving pressure difference is gone and the flow stops. You have to fill the tube again.

I came across the sourdough mid-rise. It was Thursday. Once again. It's always Thursday, always sitting on top of the flour bin, and there's always a copy of Monte Cristo in there. The copy has a stamp from the Richmond Public Library. No idea how they get through the squeaky screen door without me hearing it. Around 3 AM, my brain is pretty much just yeast and caffeine.
But tonight, there was a scrap of yellow legal paper poking out of the top of the book like a bookmark. I cleaned my hands on the apron. It leaves this white smudge on my dark apron. I pulled the paper out. It said page 142, written in spiky handwriting. It says, "Please. I think they're watching the drop box now." A cold draft swept through my kitchen. It smelled of wet asphalt and rain. I looked at the dark front windows and saw only my reflection, my tired reflection. I didn't open the book. I carefully tucked the note back between the pages. I slid the book into a brown pastry bag, folded the top down twice and sealed it.

Three stars. 38 dollars for a used mechanical keyboard. I think I got 38 dollars worth, maybe a bit more. Spacebar is super loose. Rattles every time I hit it. Not a click, a clatter, like a tray of cutlery being nudged. During the day I don't really notice it, but late at night it sounds pretty obnoxious. E key repeats itself sometimes. Once every few paragraphs I'm stuck proofreading. Meeting becomes meeeting.

I messaged the seller to ask what switches it used. Brown switches for the record. Didn't get a reply till a full week later, and the keyboard was already here. So the communication was pretty slow.

Now I could have just shipped it back. But honestly the hassle didn't seem worth it. And I'm just as happy with it, because I find it really comfortable. The keys have a nice cushioned feel, I can write long emails, no complaints from my wrists. So its a win.

Hi everyone, I didn't get to meet you before. I'm [Name], Tom's brother. The rooming situation. A bunk bed. That's how Tom was until he was 14. Been watching Tom for years. Snoring, fights over who gets the top bunk, early signs of how dependable he is. Tom is the kind of person you can count on. I once forgot my passport and he drove six hours to get it to me. He's loyal, generous. The type who will go an unreasonable distance to save you from your own stupidity. And I'm happy. You've found someone who loves you the same way we do. And unlike me, it's on a voluntary basis.

Unbiased I'd say 4 stars, personal 2.5. Never seen a Cirque du Soleil before, Le Reve was first. Expected lots of backflips and extreme acrobatics, got a lot less of that, much more interpretive dancing. Abilities are undeniably impressive, but it's just not my style. If you really like this kind of theatrical spectacle you'd probably like Le Reve. For me, I wouldn't pay more than 100 dollars. Luckily I got free tickets so I didn't pay.

Old school attendance registers are pretty good for reconstructing daily life stuff that official narratives just skip. They show you who was there or not, how consistent attendance was, sometimes even why a kid missed school. From that you can infer things like seasonal work demands, illness, bad weather, poverty, family stuff, moving, or local emergencies. They'll also show you gaps by gender, age, neighbourhood or social class. This lets researchers see how education fit into work, household routines and community expectations. Look at enough years and you'll see how schooling habits and public health changed. Main limit is they only record what the school decided to write down. They barely explain children's experiences and absences can be misreported, incomplete or just based on what the teachers assumed. So you need to compare them with other sources.

Thursdays at 2:17, she finds the library book on the bakery's back step. Always the same one. A Field Guide to North American Moths, library sticker ghost-pale on the spine, some flour worked into the jacket as if the book was helping. She returned it twice. The librarians would smile too politely. By the third week she just left it, put it beside the rye starter and said nothing.

Tonight it rained. Rain ticked on the alley door, ovens breathing. She was working croissants, pressing butter into dough with her palms, when the latch gave that tiny guilty click. No one there. Just the book, dry as a bone on the wet concrete.

Wiped hands on apron and opened it. A slip of paper between "Luna Moth" and "Promethea," folded once. Your window is the only light on this street. I read here until the first bus. I'm sorry about the crumbs.

She looked out at the alley, dented milk crates, steam off the drains. For a second the city felt enormous, then it didn't. She tore a corner from an order pad, wrote: Cinnamon rolls come out at 4:05. Put the note inside the book, left it on the warm windowsill, unlocked the back door.

We did a project in class on folded cardboard bridge designs. Built them from the same cardboard, short beam, archy stuff, and triangular folds. Tried to keep dimensions consistent and set them between supports, then added weight bit by bit. Watched them bend, tip over, or fall apart. Results? Triangular folds held weight more steadily. So fold geometry seems to matter for stability. But remember, it was handmade with a small sample size and classroom conditions. So don't go treating this as proper engineering data. Just a little observation exercise.

Book was under the bench where bread peels hang, on the steel table back door. Marguerite found it, it's a field guide to coastal birds. Cover had a stamp from the Harbor Street branch with a due date in March. The mail slot in that door had been nailed shut years ago, but the hatch next to it is where flour man used to deliver. That one never latched properly. Eleven Thursdays. She asked the day staff, checked the hatch for scratches, once stayed past four with her coat on. Nothing. The book turned up between two and four. She was always at the ovens, back to the door, when it did.

Tonight receipt from Pell's was folded into the page on oystercatchers. Ink was blotchy where someone pressed too hard. And it was a note written on it. I keep meaning to take this back to the library. Then I pass your door and there's the smell of bread and I put it down instead. Can stop if you want. Whoever it was, she thought. They smelled of salt. And it was the pages that smelled of salt. She took a pencil from her apron. Wrote on the back of the receipt. Bring it Thursday, I'll have a roll. She tucked it in at the oystercatchers page. Put the book on the hatch ledge. Bagged a warm roll and put it next to it.

I live in Toronto now, no more Hydro Ottawa, but I want to warn consumers about their alarming billing practices. I held an account for a year in a downtown apartment. I cancelled my account to move back in with my parents and pay for my MA. Despite the cancellation, Hydro Ottawa continued siphoning payments from my separate bank account at random intervals for over a year. I kept calling to tell them, sent proof of the withdrawals, but they insisted my account was closed and no debits were happening. The truth came out only when my parents and I cross-referenced our bills, it turned out that they had linked my banking details to my parents' billing number, simply because I'd mentioned moving home. My parents didn't notice because they got refunds as they overpaid often, so it seemed normal. It took me hours on the phone, I had to speak with multiple reps, and it was a manager who finally investigated. And they confirmed the error and addressed it. It was shocking, they initially refused a refund, only an apology. Never again am I going to give banking details for automatic debit. This reckless handling of our data should worry all of us.

3:40 am second rye batch still proofing. Marisol finds that library book again on the flour bin by the back door, plastic jacket cold from the alley. Fourth Thursday straight that book showed up. Its due three weeks ago, stamped Eastgate Branch. Every Thursday she carries it to the drop box on her way home. Every Thursday it comes back, like the building itself borrows it. She wiped her hands on her apron, opened the book and a folded index card slides out of the barn owls page. It says leave the vent fan on, the alley smells like bread until five. She walks her mother's dog now, mother can't anymore. Admits keeping forgetting to return it, maybe she's not wanting to. Initials R. Read it twice while the oven timer counted down. Outside fan hums, pushing warm air into the dark. She flips the card over, marks Rye's out at 4:15 with her grease pencil she uses for trays. Tors a heel off yesterday's loaf, wraps it in wax paper, places book on top, props the back door open about an inch.

So I used to fly Ryanair when I was a broke student, my ex was living in Sweden, and this was the cheapest option. The whole thing was awful. At the airport they took my £20 L’Occitane shower gel, said it was over the liquid limit, which it wasn't. They said buy me a 100ml bottle from the airport pharmacy and come back. So I did. Came back, and they had no idea what I was talking about. Brilliant. £20 gone, I was really angry. And then at the gate they charged me another £5 for a bottle of water, which I had bought inside the airport. Ryanair later stopped the Liverpool John Lennon to Stockholm Skavsta route, so now I fly Norwegian. Their customer service is poor too, but the planes feel newer and less outdated than Ryanair.

Don't think you're alone with this. I got it bad on Tuesday, huge downpour. By Thursday half my Brandywines split. You can see the seam running down the side of the fruit. It's the same story, dry spell then a deluge. The inside soaks up water faster than the skin can stretch. Sungolds are holding out more so far but I've got a few of them that look like they'll follow the Brandywines. You can't avoid the weather once it happens. The only thing that helps a bit is that two day schedule you have on a more even footing. But once the sky lets it all out at once it doesn't matter much. You should get a fair crop from the rest of the vines. Pick the split ones and put them to other uses. It's more of a headache with Brandywines, that thick skin is a liability in a storm like this. You might get better luck with Sungolds if you keep them from getting that much water in a single go.

College Board are so full of hypocrisy. My friend took a one hour SAT Subject Test, proctor gave room about twenty extra minutes. She knew the fairness of the test was compromised. So she reported it using the hotline. And the result is this huge institutional unfairness. They investigated and said no evidence of proctor or other students misconduct, but they said she had sufficient evidence and they canceled her scores. So they let the proctor off the hook and punish the honest person. Which shows you how broken the whole system is.

Pro price change. From Jan 1 2027 it moves from $12 a month to $15. You will see the change on your next invoice. If you are on an annual plan that you already paid for, your old $12 rate sticks around until the renewal date. The new figure doesn't show up until then. No action needed to keep your current rate for the term you already signed up for. The full breakdown of new rates is in the pricing section of your account, and that page will show exactly when your renewal falls. If that date lands on or after Jan 1, you get moved to $15. We send a reminder in the months before it so you have time to look at your options. Most answers are in the help center. So that's probably faster than emailing me. But let me know if you have questions about how it works for your setup. Best, Dan

So every Thursday that book comes back. It's wedged behind the flour bins by the back door. Not on the counter. Whoever leaves it knows I'll never trip over it. It's always that same book, "A Field Guide to North American Moths", Elmwood Branch. The due date is stamped so long ago the ink's gone violet. I've never actually seen anyone drop it off. By two I'm elbow-deep in rye dough, and honestly at that hour I wouldn't notice a marching band. The first few weeks I just set it on the shelf by the register and by Friday morning it was gone. Thursday, back again. Fine. People are strange. I'm a guy who talks to his sourdough starter so I'm not judging. But tonight there's a note tucked at page 114, the luna moths. The note says they only live a week. They don't even eat. The author wonders if it's a waste of a beautiful thing and asks if I ever get to see the bread before it's gone. No signature, just pencil pressed hard. I read it twice then a third time while the ovens ticked. Then I pulled the first loaf of the night, still crackling, wrapped it in brown paper, and set it behind the flour bins.

Stuffy rooms aren't just about the temperature, even if it is comfortable. If humidity is high, skin moisture doesn't evaporate. So the air feels heavy and stale. The air movement matters too. If it doesn't move, the air doesn't move, the carbon dioxide from our breathing, the smell, heat, the air doesn't move. So it lingers in the room. Ventilation poor, it feels close and oppressive. And when aircon on, it might feel cool, but it doesn't necessarily reduce the humidity, and it doesn't improve the circulation. Opening up a window, having a fan, having ventilation, it feels fresher. So it does feel fresher because the air is moving, it's lower humidity.

I spent two years mentoring five junior engineers and I do not buy the idea that remote work is good for everyone. These folks don't need tickets, docs, scheduled meetings. What they need is to be in the design arguments, see someone solve a nasty bug, get answers before their uncertainty snowballs. That stuff you get free in an office. At home you have to figure out when to interrupt, get a call set up, and explain a problem they probably don't get yet. Steep thing to ask of someone new who hasn't had the chance to learn it. So I watched that setup screw up the feedback. A short note on a code review starts reading like a final judgment. The lag getting answers kills forward motion. When they could pair up in person, work on the whiteboard, and actually get hold of the seniors, the juniors moved ahead a lot quicker. None of this means scrap flexibility. It works fine for people who can direct their own efforts. For a beginner, being around other people is how you get the confidence, context, judgment. Otherwise you hand a newcomer a laptop and a calendar, and down the road you end up with weaker technical leadership.

A rain gauge is really basic. Its an open tube. You put it outside, rain falls in, and it tells you depth. Millimetres, inches. Its just how deep the water would be if nothing got away. Not drain, not evaporate, not soak into the ground. Most are a funnel setup. Big opening, small tube, and it's scaled. So you can see small amounts easier. If the area ratio is accounted for in the scale, it's still accurate. Wind is a problem. It blows past the opening, so you get undercounted. If you dont read it quickly, you lose to evaporation, or splashing.

Got this keyboard second hand for $38. As soon as I opened it, that price felt fair. Dust between the keys, shiny spots on the caps, but expected for used. The comfort is genuinely good. I type long emails at work and my hands dont feel as cramped as my flat office board. Switches feel steady, not too heavy. Case sits firm, no sliding around. But problems. The space bar rattles every hit, loud in quiet mornings. The "e" key occasionally repeats, types neeed when I type fast. Not constantly, but enough I proofread more. Seller was slow on my question about switches, answered a full week after I already had it. Not great. Still kept it for $38. Shipping back felt more trouble than its worth.

One broken item per person, bring it along. You'll grab a numbered ticket at the front table and just keep it till it's fixed. They'll call numbers in order and they need you around, especially if something's a judgment call. Not everything can be fixed, parts might need ordering, some won't be possible. Pick your stuff up before the volunteers leave at 4:30, if you don't, it's gone, can't be stored.

Went Friday around 4:30 pm. No line. Total bill for two was about $130. I had expected to pay a steakhouse price and it cost me more. I was upset steak wasn't there. At that price, I really wanted some kind of steak. There was lamb, prime rib, chicken. Things I can get at other Vegas buffets for less money. Seafood had Alaska crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaska crab legs are common. Rock crab claws I've not seen elsewhere and it was interesting. Problem was no claw crackers. They said mallets were available. Our table was really close to the next table and I didn't want to smack crab shells and have it flinging at the people next to us. So I just ate crab legs. Asian station was not very distinctive. It was similar to Rampart Casino buffet. Dessert had gelato, pastries, fresh juice. Nothing special. I did not try juice. I think it was acceptable. Overpriced. Worth trying once. If no line. Long line, reconsider.

Old attendance registers are a goldmine for me. They log daily life for me. Seasons matter. If kids disappear for harvest or flu or snow, it's all in the logs. The patterns tell us about the community. If the teachers or headmasters are fudging the numbers, I'll know. They'd need to justify a drop if a local outbreak or harvest happens. And I'll also notice if there's consistent absenteeism from some groups of kids. The absence of the children will point to cultural attitudes or social inequalities. The issue is that the records can be faked. A teacher might just mark them present to get funding or avoid scrutiny. But registers don't tell you why the kids are missing. You have to cross-reference with other sources. It's a quantitative framework. But you need other evidence. The numbers aren't always reality. I need to dig into the social structure.

I've got a personal take on Apple and I really do think they deserve a mention. When I was at school we were only allowed Apple laptops, and they cost double anything else. They were breaking around once a month for me. I never dropped my laptop even once, but in the four years that I had it, I changed the hard drive five times. Reinstalled the OS several times just to get it working. A friend's MacBook Pro actually caught fire once while watching a movie. The smoke alarm went off. And Apple support never actually diagnosed anything, they'd just back up the computer, wipe it and restore the files. Same with the iPhones, I had the first iPhone and it was malfunctioning all the time. And now they release a new one every two months and it's like only the camera is a bit better than the previous one. But I'll give them credit that their iPads are the best tablets currently. Though I think Android tablets will catch up at some point.

So basically the trough has a float valve connected to a pressure water line. There's a float on the surface, like a ball or block, that sits on a lever. Cattle drink, level goes down, float drops, tilts the arm so it pulls the plunger or washer off the seat and water flows in. Then as water fills the trough, the float goes up and pushes the plunger back against the seat. It closes in stages until it's shut off at the set level. Overflow, which happens all the time, is because of a worn or dirty washer that doesn't seal. Or the float gets a hole and fills with water, doesn't lift enough to close it.
